sents: Today’s AI is mostly trained in a similar manner: when the AI gives a reply, a scoring agent working from a rubric considers whether it is helpful to the user.
Does it make the user more likely to accept it?
Which is whether the user will be happy.
And even when humans score the replies themselves, every turn they evaluate whether they are happy with the result.
As emergent behaviour, this may lead to the outcome the human needed.
But it is a struggle.
And it’s very easy for AI to lose sight of what the user wants to achieve in the long run, over the whole conversation.
Once the goal is out of sight, the model makes a mistake I see more often than any other: it takes what is important for what is relevant.
The two are different.
Whether something is important depends on the thing itself.
Whether it is relevant depends on what you are trying to achieve.
A person who goes to work knows this without being told.
You don’t walk in and say, my child has been diagnosed with a disease.
Is that important?
Of course it is.
Is it relevant to the work?
No.
A model has no such sense, because without the goal it has only importance to go by.
A company found that for more than half a year it had been overpaying into its staff’s retirement fund, because it had misread a regulation.
That is serious, and once the model knew about it, it could not stop bringing it up, even when negotiating with a supplier or briefing a lawyer on a matter that had nothing to do with it.

batches.assembled_prompt:
The intended reader has read the essay's introduction, which lists seven pillars, the behaviours an AI employee needs, and this chapter up to the passage below. The chapter is about the first pillar, play for the goal. It opened with the story of a kitten that keeps dropping its fishing rod to chase dragonflies, and argued that a model trained to do well at every reply is optimised the same way, one moment at a time. The passage below follows a section on why training that scores each step falls short when the real result comes only at the end. The intended reader reads as an editor who listens closely for how the text moves from one sentence to the next.

The text, each paragraph starting with its number:

[P1] Today’s AI is mostly trained in a similar manner: when the AI gives a reply, a scoring agent working from a rubric considers whether it is helpful to the user. Does it make the user more likely to accept it? Which is whether the user will be happy. And even when humans score the replies themselves, every turn they evaluate whether they are happy with the result. As emergent behaviour, this may lead to the outcome the human needed. But it is a struggle. And it’s very easy for AI to lose sight of what the user wants to achieve in the long run, over the whole conversation.

[P2] Once the goal is out of sight, the model makes a mistake I see more often than any other: it takes what is important for what is relevant. The two are different. Whether something is important depends on the thing itself. Whether it is relevant depends on what you are trying to achieve. A person who goes to work knows this without being told. You don’t walk in and say, my child has been diagnosed with a disease. Is that important? Of course it is. Is it relevant to the work? No. A model has no such sense, because without the goal it has only importance to go by. A company found that for more than half a year it had been overpaying into its staff’s retirement fund, because it had misread a regulation. That is serious, and once the model knew about it, it could not stop bringing it up, even when negotiating with a supplier or briefing a lawyer on a matter that had nothing to do with it.

Score each sentence on the offence below. A score is roughly how many intended readers in ten would meet the problem at that sentence (0 = none, 9 = nearly all).

1. Unmarked turn: for a sentence that turns from stating a point to illustrating it with a generic person, company or scene, score 0 to 9 how likely the intended reader is to want words that mark the turn, such as "Consider…", "Take…" or "For example…".

Spelling and grammar do not count.

Write a TSV and nothing else. One row per sentence where the score is 2 or more, in reading order: paragraph.sentence (e.g. 3.2), TAB, the score, TAB, why. Keep why to at most 15 words. Last line: END.
